title: Foundations of Game QA
summary: Quality assurance vs. testing, tester duties, defect vs. failure, and professional ethics.
explanation: Quality Assurance (QA) defines the proactive processes that prevent defects, while Software Testing executes the game to discover defects. Testers do not 'break' games; they expose pre-existing failures to safeguard player trust and experience.
example: Example: If a character falls through the terrain during an inventory toggle, the root cause is an error in code or bounding geometry. The defect exists in the build; the failure occurs when the character plunges into empty space.
activity: Try this: Note three differences between checking if an attack animation runs vs. evaluating whether the combat feels responsive and satisfying.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between a defect and a failure?
quiz.a: A defect (bug) is an imperfection or flaw in code/assets. A failure is the observable deviation in game behavior when that flawed code executes.

title: Test Design & Technique
summary: Objectives, preconditions, boundary analysis, equivalence partitioning, and risk.
explanation: Structured test design prevents random guessing. Equivalence partitioning divides inputs into groups treated similarly (e.g., valid inventory quantities 1 to 99). Boundary value analysis focuses on edges (0, 1, 99, 100), where game loops most frequently fail.
example: Example: Testing an ammo clip of 30 rounds. Test boundaries: 0 (empty), 1 (minimum), 30 (full capacity), and 31 (overflow attempt via reload prompt).
activity: Try this: Create test boundaries for a player character's age selector configured to accept ages 13 to 99.

quiz.q: Why do boundaries fail more often than interior values?
quiz.a: Programmers frequently make off-by-one comparison errors (e.g., using '<' instead of '<=', or array index offsets starting at 0).

title: Clear Bug Reports
summary: Reproduction steps, expected vs. actual behavior, severity, priority, and evidence.
explanation: A high-quality bug report allows any developer to replicate the issue on their first attempt without asking clarification questions. Severity defines how severely the flaw harms game mechanics; Priority indicates how urgently management needs it patched.
example: Example Title: '[Shop UI] Tapping Purchase button 5 times rapidly charges gold multiple times for single potion'.
activity: Try this: Review a vague bug report like 'Sound is broken' and rewrite it into a precise, actionable summary with steps.

quiz.q: Can a bug have high severity but low priority?
quiz.a: Yes. An instant crash occurring exclusively when an obscure legacy controller is unplugged during the end-game credits has Critical Severity (crash) but Low Priority (unlikely edge case close to deadline).

title: Game Feature Testing
summary: Controls, rules, physics, scoring, UI, save/load cycles, and audio cues.
explanation: Games contain non-linear, stateful systems. Feature testing checks both discrete logic (scoring arithmetic, inventory persistence) and sensory feedback (sound effects syncing with sword strikes, menu navigation).
example: Example: Verifying pause states. If an explosion initiates when Pause is clicked, physics particles, hitboxes, and timer sounds must completely halt until Resume is clicked.
activity: Try this: Outline 4 test conditions for saving a game mid-combat, closing the app, and relaunching.

quiz.q: What makes game save/load testing uniquely challenging?
quiz.a: Save data must serialize vast dynamic states (coordinates, AI aggro, quest progression, physics momentum) accurately across software updates.

title: Mobile & Platform Coverage
summary: Device matrices, OS fragmentation, interruptions, thermal throttling, and screen ratios.
explanation: Mobile titles operate in hostile device environments. Testing must account for incoming phone calls, low battery notifications, aspect ratio cutoffs (notches, hole punches), and backgrounding.
example: Example: Receiving a phone call during an active multiplayer match. Does the game reconnect smoothly or freeze the entire device UI?
activity: Try this: Test an app while transitioning your phone from Wi-Fi to airplane mode and back.

quiz.a: Testing how gracefully the game suspends and restores state when interrupted by device events like calls, SMS overlays, alarms, or OS prompts.

title: Retesting & Release Readiness
summary: Regression testing, smoke runs, sanity verification, release notes, and risk sign-off.
explanation: Retesting verifies that a specific defect has been resolved. Regression testing verifies that the developer's fix did not inadvertently break other existing features. Smoke testing provides a quick health check before committing builds to wider QA.
example: Example: Fixing a weapon reload bug could accidentally alter all animation timing. QA retests reload (Retest) and conducts a quick run of combat and mobility (Regression).
activity: Try this: Write a 5-item smoke test checklist for a game build before it is handed to full QA.

quiz.q: Why is regression testing essential after every bug fix?
quiz.a: Game code is highly interdependent; altering physics, memory, or UI logic in one subsystem frequently causes unintended side effects elsewhere.

title: Session 1: Foundations of Game Testing
summary: Games and gamification, the tester?s role, and the main types of game testing.
explanation: A game combines players, rules, objectives and feedback in voluntary play. Gamification applies game elements such as points or challenges to a non-game activity. Game testing is a structured investigation of game quality: testers compare behavior with expectations, record evidence and communicate findings throughout development, from planning to post-launch support. Functional testing checks mechanics against requirements; UI/UX testing examines navigation and usability; playtesting explores the player experience, balance and pacing; compatibility testing covers relevant devices, operating systems and displays.
example: A mobile game has a working purchase button (functional), but its label is cut off on a small screen (UI/UX). Players find the tutorial confusing (playtesting), and the layout differs on another device (compatibility).
activity: Choose a game and write one test idea for each of the four testing types. Identify the device or player context for each idea.

quiz.q: How does playtesting differ from functional testing?
quiz.a: Functional testing checks whether features behave as intended; playtesting investigates the player experience, including enjoyment, balance and pacing.

title: Session 2: Mobile Bug Identification & Reporting
summary: Spot visual and functional issues and document reproducible mobile bug reports.
explanation: Look for visual anomalies such as missing textures, overlapping controls or stuttering animations, and functional issues such as unresponsive controls, broken rules, crashes or frame drops. Explore with a purpose, vary relevant boundaries and conditions, and use regression testing to check that existing behavior still works after changes. A useful report includes a specific title, preconditions and numbered reproduction steps, expected and actual results, device and build details, severity, and evidence. Record network conditions and frequency when relevant; protect personal information in evidence.
example: Example scenario: On a test Android device, collecting a power-up in level 3 freezes and closes the game. State the app build and device, list the steps from launch to collection, describe the expected power-up effect and the observed freeze and crash, and attach a recording if available.
activity: Find an issue in a game you can test. Write a report with a specific title, numbered steps, expected and actual results, environment, severity and privacy-safe evidence. Attempt to reproduce it and record the frequency.

quiz.q: What environment information helps someone reproduce a mobile bug?
quiz.a: Record the device model, OS version and app version or build; include relevant display, network and other conditions, as well as reproduction frequency.
